passage: Himani, sit. I am Sarita, and you asked why I never fight with your Uncle Rohit over the house papers, so I'll tell you. When I was twenty-five, Amma and Baba bought Rohit a motorbike for passing one exam. My first-class degree got a sweet and a pat on the head. Then came the talk about the will, and Baba said, "Rohit will need more, he's a boy." I sat in the kitchen while my tea went cold, feeling like furniture. I could have shouted at Rohit. He hadn't asked for any of it. Instead, one evening I told Amma, quietly, "It hurts when my work goes unseen." She went silent, then said she hadn't realised. It didn't fix everything. But I stopped waiting for applause and took the evening course I'd wanted. Rohit and I still share Diwali dinners. That mattered more than winning an argument would have.

qa.q: What did Amma and Baba buy Rohit for passing one exam?
How did Sarita feel in the kitchen while the tea went cold?
qa.a: Sarita felt like furniture, unseen and hurt, yet did not blame Rohit, who hadn't asked for any of it.

qa.q: What did Sarita do instead of turning it into a fight with Rohit?
qa.a: Sarita told Amma quietly that it hurts when work goes unseen, took the evening course Sarita had wanted, and kept sharing Diwali dinners with Rohit.

qa.q: How might Amma have experienced Sarita's quiet words?
qa.a: Amma went silent and then said she hadn't realised, which suggests Amma had not noticed the hurt until it was said calmly.

grounding: An adult child feels unseen by parents who favour a sibling, says so calmly, avoids war with the sibling and builds worth through their own course.

passage:
Sunday. Ammi's birthday lunch.

Faisal got a new watch from Abbu. In front of everyone. "For my son who makes me proud." I got a pat on the shoulder. I've been sending half my salary home for three years. Faisal still borrows from them.

I smiled through the biryani, then went and sat on the stairs for a while so no one would see my face. I felt invisible, like the extra chair at the table.

What I'm not going to do: pick a fight with Faisal. It's not his watch that hurts. It's Abbu's words.

What I might do: talk to Ammi quietly next week, maybe on our evening walk. Just say, "I felt unseen today." No accusations.

In the evening I went to cricket with Pankaj and the office team. I hit two fours and everyone cheered like idiots. That helped more than I expected.

I'm Wasim, their son too. I'm allowed to be enough without the watch.

qa.q: What did Abbu give Faisal at the birthday lunch?
qa.a: He gave Faisal a new watch.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel sitting on the stairs?
qa.a: Wasim felt invisible and hurt, like the extra chair at the table.

qa.q: What wise choices does Wasim make in the entry?
qa.a: He decides not to fight with Faisal, plans to tell Ammi calmly that he felt unseen, and builds his worth through friends and cricket.

qa.q: How might Faisal have experienced the lunch?
qa.a: Faisal may simply have enjoyed the gift and not noticed his brother's hurt at all.

grounding: A diary entry shows a young man whose parents openly favour his brother, feeling unseen and hurt, choosing a calm word with a parent over war with his sibling.

passage:
Shalini: they read Papa's will out today
Minakshi: and?
Shalini: flat goes to Bhaiya. Gold goes to Bhaiya's wife. I get "Shalini will be looked after by her husband"
Minakshi: wow. How are you feeling
Shalini: like I was never really part of the family 😔 like 26 years of being the good daughter meant nothing
Minakshi: that's awful. I'm so sorry 🫂
Shalini: part of me wants to call Bhaiya and scream
Minakshi: is he the one who wrote it though?
Shalini: no. He looked embarrassed honestly
Minakshi: then maybe save the fight for where it belongs
Shalini: Mummy. I think I'll tell her how it felt. Calmly. Not about the flat, about being seen
Minakshi: that sounds right. And you're so much more than what's in that will
Shalini: I know. My design studio is mine. Nobody wrote that for me 🙂

qa.q: What does the will say about Shalini?
qa.a: It says "Shalini will be looked after by her husband".

qa.q: How does Shalini feel after hearing the will?
qa.a: Shalini feels hurt and unseen, as if twenty-six years of being the good daughter meant nothing.

qa.q: How does Minakshi help Shalini respond wisely?
qa.a: She asks whether her brother wrote it, which helps Shalini avoid a war with him and choose to tell her mother calmly.

qa.q: How might Shalini's brother have felt when the will was read?
qa.a: He looked embarrassed, so he may feel awkward and uneasy about being favoured over his sister.

grounding: A chat shows a young woman hurt by her parents' favouritism in a will, who chooses to speak calmly to her mother, not fight her brother, and finds worth in her own work.
